theory.text: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1
A step-by-step self-study guide
Learn the theory • Practise short skills • Plan the information • Write a complete report

This guide covers charts, tables, maps and processes for IELTS Academic. Task 1 is a report describing visual information. Work through the stages in order, then return to the skills that need more practice.
Your learning route

rows: Learn what to select, how to organise it and which language to use.
Complete E1–E7 before checking your answers.
Plan W1–W11 without writing full reports.
Plan, write and revise Tasks 1–27 using the original visuals.
Compare your work with the explanations, plans and model reports.
All answers are at the end.

theory.text: A study routine you can repeat

Session 1: Read one theory section and complete a related short exercise. Session 2: Plan two visuals using the worksheet. Session 3: Write one complete report. Session 4: Check it, record your errors and rewrite the weakest paragraph. Begin untimed; later use the 20-minute routine in Part 4.

Keep longer responses in a notebook or separate document. The response lines are for brief notes. Suggested answers are examples of valid approaches, not scripts to memorise or examiner-awarded band scores.

Part 1 Theory
Know the task and the report structure
Write at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. Use full sentences and connected paragraphs in a neutral or academic style. Task 2 contributes twice as much as Task 1 to the Writing score. [1]

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Suppose a chart shows the proportion of commuters using buses and bicycles in two cities in 2010 and 2020. A suitable report would introduce those two modes and places, summarise the strongest overall contrast, and then give selected numbers.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The job is to REPORT the information, not argue that cycling is healthier. First name the subject, place and period; next choose the two biggest patterns for the overview; finally support them with the chart values. This shows how a selective 150-word report differs from an opinion essay.
Your job: select, summarise and compare

Report what the visual shows. Include the main features and enough detail to support them. Do not add personal opinions, background knowledge or reasons that the visual does not establish. A higher birth rate and a younger population may appear together; the table alone does not prove one caused the other.

rows: Visual type, topic, place, time and units where relevant. Paraphrase accurately.
Two or three main trends, contrasts, changes or process features.
Selected figures, comparisons, locations or stages.
The remaining main features, with supporting detail.

theory.text: Four paragraphs are a useful starting point, not a compulsory rule. The overview can follow the introduction or come at the end. A separate opinion or argumentative conclusion is unnecessary.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Illustrative chart: in City A, cycling increases from 10% to 30%, while bus use falls from 50% to 35%. In City B, cycling stays near 15%. Overview: “Cycling became substantially more common in City A, while City B showed little change.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The example selects the standout development and the contrast rather than listing every percentage. “Became more common” is a description of the shown data; “because the council built new paths” would be an invented cause unless it appears in the visual.
Introduction versus overview
Introduction: “The chart compares the proportions of male and female teachers in six types of UK educational institution in 2010.” This identifies the task.
Overview: “Women formed the large majority in nursery and primary education, whereas men predominated at university level. College teaching staff were evenly divided.” This selects the main features.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Question: a bar chart compares renewable electricity shares in four countries in 2015 and 2025. Introduction: “The bar chart compares the proportion of electricity generated from renewable sources in four countries in 2015 and 2025.” Overview: “All four shares increased, with Country A remaining the highest in both years.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The introduction tells a reader WHAT the graphic displays: type, measure, groups and dates. The overview states the main PATTERNS and ranking. Notice that it does not require exact percentages; save the supporting values for the body paragraphs.
What the four assessment criteria mean

Task Achievement: accurate coverage, clear overview and relevant support. Coherence and Cohesion: logical grouping and clear connections. Lexical Resource: precise vocabulary. Grammatical Range and Accuracy: varied, controlled sentences. [1, 2]
Vietnamese reminder: tổng quan = bức tranh lớn; chi tiết = số liệu hoặc đặc điểm minh họa. Do not turn the overview into a list of every value.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Draft: “Bikes improved a lot. City A 10, 30. Buses were worse.” Revised: “In City A, the share of bicycle commuters rose from 10% to 30%, while bus use fell from 50% to 35%.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Task Achievement improves because both trends and values are clear; Coherence improves through the “while” contrast; Lexical Resource improves through “share” and “rose”; Grammar improves through complete, controlled clauses. A polished sentence still needs an overall overview elsewhere in the report.
Describe change accurately

rows: There was a rise in sales from 20 to 30.
There was a fall in sales to 15.
There was a recovery in sales.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Illustrative line graph: online purchases account for 10%, 12%, 25% and 27% in successive years. Description: “The proportion rose slightly at first, then increased sharply before levelling off.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Match the adjective or adverb to EACH interval: 10→12 is small, 12→25 is large, and 25→27 is small again. “Rose steadily” would conceal the faster middle stage. Do not use “fluctuated” unless values actually move up and down.
Combine the direction with the size or speed

Verb + adverb: rose gradually; fell sharply. Adjective + noun: a gradual rise; a sharp fall. “Steady” describes a consistent pattern; “stable” describes little change. A series that falls once has not necessarily fluctuated.

Use strong words such as “soared” or “plummeted” only for clearly large, rapid changes. Prefer “rose” or “fell” when the pattern is ordinary. A fall from 7,000 to 5,000 is roughly 29%, so calling it “slight” may be misleading.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Values: monthly visitors rise from 2,000 in January to 2,150 in February and 5,800 in March. “Visitor numbers increased marginally in February, before rising sharply in March.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  “Increased” and “rising” identify direction; “marginally” and “sharply” describe magnitude. If the time intervals are equal, speed may also be inferred, but do not claim that a small increase was “dramatic”. The word choice should be calibrated to the scale.
Keep prepositions clear

From 23% to 46% = the starting and ending values. To 46% = the ending value. By 23 percentage points = the difference between the percentages. Between 1990 and 2000 = the time span; do not write “between 1990 to 2000”.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  A city’s cycling share was 18% in 2012 and 33% in 2022. Correct: “It rose FROM 18% TO 33%, an increase OF 15 percentage points, BETWEEN 2012 AND 2022.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  FROM introduces the starting level; TO introduces the ending level; OF introduces the size of the rise; BETWEEN … AND … sets the time span. The share did not rise “to 15%”, and “by 15%” would wrongly suggest a relative percentage increase.
Percentage points are different from percentage change

A share rising from 23% to 46% increases by 23 percentage points. The relative increase is 100% because (46 − 23) ÷ 23 × 100 = 100. The share doubles. “It increased by 23%” would describe a different calculation.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Example data: a pass rate increases from 40% to 50%. Percentage-point rise = 50 − 40 = 10 points. Relative percentage rise = (50 − 40) ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The two answers are not interchangeable: “rose by 10 percentage points” discusses the gap between shares, while “rose by 25%” discusses the size of that gap relative to the original 40%. If unsure, report “rose from 40% to 50%” instead.
Combine two stages of a trend

“The number of factories rose to 120,000 in 2010 before falling to 10,000 in 2015.” Or: “After reaching 120,000 in 2010, the number of factories fell to 10,000 five years later.” Keep the subject clear after an introductory phrase.
Avoid unnatural phrases such as “recorded with 23%” or “the quantity witnessed a wild oscillation”. Clear alternatives are “The figure stood at 23%” and “The number fluctuated considerably”.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Values: app users total 15,000 in 2018, 45,000 in 2021 and 30,000 in 2023. “User numbers tripled between 2018 and 2021, before declining to 30,000 in 2023.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The sentence compresses two genuine stages into one readable comparison: expansion followed by contraction. “Tripled” is justified because 45,000 equals three times 15,000. The final 30,000 is lower than the peak but still above the initial figure.
Compare quantities without changing the meaning

rows: the number of people / cars / factories
the percentage of time spent online
the number of users, if only time shares are shown
The figure for Australia was higher than that for Spain.
fewer teachers; less water; a lower percentage
the largest share; 39% was the largest category
the majority, when the share is below 50%

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Illustrative table: 60% of adults drink tea daily, against 45% who drink coffee daily. “Tea was consumed daily by 15 percentage points more adults than coffee.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The subjects remain comparable (shares of adults). The difference is 60−45 = 15 percentage points. Do not write “15% more people” if you mean percentage points, or say tea was “twice as popular” when the ratio is only 60:45.
Four useful comparison patterns
Australia received about 41,000 British emigrants, compared with 35,000 in Spain.
About 41,000 people moved to Australia, while around 35,000 chose Spain.
The figure for Australia was about 6,000 higher than that for Spain.
Around 41,000 and 35,000 British people moved to Australia and Spain respectively.
“While” and “whereas” introduce contrasting clauses. They do not require a comparative adjective. “Compared with” is followed by a noun phrase or figure; it also does not require “higher” or “lower”.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  City X has 80 public parks and City Y has 50. (1) “City X had 80 parks, compared with 50 in City Y.” (2) “City X had 30 more parks than City Y.” (3) “While X had 80, Y had 50.” (4) “X and Y had 80 and 50 parks, respectively.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Each sentence preserves the same comparison while changing grammar. “More … than” requires an explicit comparable noun; “while” connects two complete clauses; “respectively” works only when the noun and number orders correspond.
Use ratios carefully

“Twice as many people” describes counts; “twice as much water” describes an amount. “Three times as high” is clearer than the ambiguous “three times higher”. If two values are 20 and 60, say “60 was three times the figure of 20”.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  A table shows 40 buses and 80 taxis. Correct: “There were twice as many taxis as buses.” A second table shows 60 litres of water versus 20 litres: “The first system used three times as much water as the second.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Countable items use “many”; uncountable quantity uses “much”. Always compute the ratio before using “twice” or “three times”. “80 taxis were twice higher” is grammatically misleading; repeat the thing counted so readers know exactly what is doubled.
Paraphrase precisely

Visitors are people; visits are occasions. Applicants are not necessarily enrolled students. Population is not population density. Income, revenue and profit are not automatically interchangeable. Keep the chart’s meaning even if you repeat a key word.
Prefer “accounted for”, “represented”, “stood at” and “was higher than”. Avoid “domineering”, “outperformed” or “outnumbered” when simply comparing percentages or hours.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Source title: “Average number of visits to museums per resident”. Safe introduction: “The chart shows the average number of museum visits made by each resident.” Unsafe: “The chart shows how many residents visited a museum.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Visits and visitors are different units: one resident can make several visits. Preserve that distinction even when the rewritten sentence repeats “visits”. Precision is more important than replacing every phrase with a new synonym.
Read charts and choose the main features
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Imaginary bar chart: four countries have recycling rates of 70%, 68%, 30% and 28%. Overview: “The first two countries recycled a markedly larger share of waste than the other two.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Rather than listing all four figures in an overview, spot the two clear clusters. In the body, group the high-rate pair and the low-rate pair and cite their values. This turns observation into a coherent report structure.
First decide whether time changes

rows: What rose, fell or changed rank? What were the main turning points?
Rising versus falling series; or earlier versus later periods.
What was highest or lowest? Where were the biggest contrasts or similarities?
Higher group versus lower group; or related categories.
What does each whole represent? Which shares dominate?
Compare the same category across pies, then other important shares.
Which rows and columns share the same units and meaning?
Group similar measures; keep money, years and percentages distinct.
What is the main message of each visual? Can they be compared directly?
Often one details paragraph per visual. Cover both in the overview.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  A bar chart showing spending on food, housing and leisure in 2022 is a static comparison. A line chart showing the same spending from 2010 to 2022 is a time series.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  For the first, compare categories and rank the shares: “Housing accounted for the largest share.” For the second, describe change and dates: “Housing spending rose over the period.” Do not invent a trend from a single snapshot.
A chart-reading checklist
Read the title, legend and all labels before looking at the values.
Identify the unit: people, thousands, millions, percentages, money, hours or volume.
Read the dates and distinguish measured figures from forecasts.
Find two or three main features, then choose supporting details.
Check whether the graphic supports exact values or only estimates.

Use “about”, “approximately”, “just over” or “just under” for values read from a scale. Exact labels in a table can be reported directly. Do not give invented precision such as 34.73% when the axis only supports about 35%.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  A vertical axis says “thousands of passengers”, with a bar at 35 for 2019. The defensible statement is “about 35,000 passengers in 2019”, not “35 passengers” or “35 million”.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Read the title and unit BEFORE forming a sentence. Next check legend, dates, and whether numbers are exact labels or estimates from the scale. These checks prevent errors in Task Achievement even when the grammar sounds fluent.
Do not force a total or a causal story

Selected categories may not add up to 100%. Report the values shown; do not invent missing categories or adjust the data. Two mixed visuals may show related changes without proving a cause. Write “Spending and participation both increased”, rather than “Participation caused spending to increase”.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  A survey reports 55% using streaming services and 40% using radio. It permits overlap: respondents may use both. Safe: “Streaming was more widely used than radio.” Unsupported: “Only 5% used neither platform.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The two percentages do not necessarily form parts of a single whole because categories may overlap. Similarly, if sales rise when advertising rises, report the parallel trends rather than asserting advertising caused the increase.
Choose tenses from the task

Finished dates: “rose”, “accounted for”. No date: “shows”, “accounts for”. A series ending at the chart’s “present day”: present perfect can summarise the whole period. Forecasts: “is projected to reach”. A forecast made in 1990 for 2000: “was predicted to reach”, followed by the actual past result.
Do not reinterpret a source’s “present day” as today’s calendar date or change a forecast into a measured fact just because time has passed.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  One table reports 2015 values; another column predicts 2035. “In 2015, solar power provided 12% of the total; it is projected to account for 35% in 2035.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Use past simple for completed observations and a projection verb for future estimates. The tense follows the information status in the chart, not today’s date. Avoid writing “rose to 35% in 2035” as if the projected outcome had already been measured.
Describe maps and proposed changes

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Two maps show a riverside park in 2000 and its proposed redesign. A playground will replace a car park, but the river and entrance will remain. Overview: “The proposal replaces vehicle space with recreation while retaining the main access and riverfront.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Group changed and unchanged features before describing locations. Use proposal language (“is planned to”, “will be built”) rather than factual past change, and mention north/south only if the map establishes direction.
Read the place before describing the changes

Find the compass, dates, entrances, roads, rivers and other fixed landmarks. Identify additions, removals, replacements, relocations and features that remain. Group details by area or by type of development.

rows: in the north-west; south of the river; opposite the school; beside the road
The factory was replaced by a car park.
The office was converted into a museum.
The school was moved to the north of the river.
The housing area was expanded; the woodland was reduced in size.
The railway station remained in the same position.
The airfield is to be replaced by an industrial estate.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  On a north-oriented map, the railway runs across the southern edge. A warehouse north of it is replaced by apartments, while the station to the east remains.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Anchor the description to stable landmarks: “North of the railway, the warehouse was replaced by housing, whereas the station in the east remained unchanged.” This is more accurate than describing items solely as “left” and “right” without checking orientation.
Write a meaningful overview

Weak: “There were many changes and the general layout stayed the same.” Stronger: “The former mining site was converted into a visitor attraction, with museums and recreational facilities replacing most working facilities.”

Only say the layout remained unchanged if the maps actually support that claim. Be specific about stable features, such as a river or a main road. Do not assume a beach had no previous use or that a new road will reduce congestion unless the task states it.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Illustrative before-and-after maps: a former industrial island gains hotels and footpaths, while a central dock stays. Overview: “The island was transformed into a tourist destination, although the central dock remained in place.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The overview tells readers what TYPE of transformation occurred and identifies a major exception. It does not catalogue each hut, path and bench. “The island became more modern” is too vague and subjective to count as a strong overview.
Choose a sensible body structure

For a town divided by a road: describe the west first, then the east. For an island: describe buildings and accommodation, then paths, access and swimming facilities. For a current plan and a proposal: compare each existing feature with its proposed replacement.
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Map: a central road separates a western housing area from an eastern business area. Western changes: houses and a playground. Eastern changes: offices and a new car park.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Write one paragraph about the west and one about the east, referring to the road as the boundary. This stops the reader mentally jumping between locations. If the task instead shows an old map versus a proposal, you could organise by replaced feature.
Use tenses naturally

Two finished dates can both use the past simple: “In 2000 there was an open space; by 2011 it had been replaced by flats.” Past perfect helps show an earlier past event, but is not required for every sentence about the earlier map. For proposals use “will be built”, “is planned” or “is proposed”.
Vietnamese reminder: vị trí → thay đổi → đặc điểm thay thế. Check the direction before choosing “north”, “south”, “left” or “right”.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Map A (1995): a field near the river. Map B (2015): a sports centre in its place. A proposed map for 2030: an extension east of that centre. “The field was replaced by a sports centre by 2015, and an extension is planned to its east.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The first change is a completed fact, so past passive “was replaced” fits. The extension is a proposal, so “is planned” avoids presenting it as completed. A past-perfect construction is optional, not a requirement for describing earlier maps.
Describe processes, cycles and anatomy

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Simplified glass-bottle process: used bottles are collected, cleaned, melted, shaped and cooled. Overview: “The process converts collected glass into new bottles through cleaning, melting and remoulding.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  This overview identifies the input, output and core transformation. Body details can group preparation (collection and washing) and manufacture (melting to cooling). Only mention machines, temperatures or durations if the diagram shows them.
Follow arrows rather than inventing stages

Identify the input, output, main stages, branches and any repeated cycle. An overview should describe the process as a whole: its start and end, or its main transformation. Count stages only when the diagram supports a clear count.

rows: Tomatoes are sorted, crushed and boiled.
Eggs hatch; larvae grow; adults lay eggs.
How is energy or fuel transferred?
Gas fuels an engine, which drives a generator.
Some juice is packaged directly; the rest is concentrated.
Where are the parts, and what is shown?
The wings lie beneath the red elytra.

theory.text: WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Diagram: harvested beans → drying → roasting → grinding → packaging. Appropriate line: “After drying, the beans are roasted and ground before they are packaged.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Read arrows as evidence for SEQUENCE. Do not describe grinding before roasting or add fermentation if absent. If a diagram splits into two production lines, describe the branch rather than pretending that all products follow one route.
Use the passive when the material is the focus
Active: “Workers remove the seeds.” Passive: “The seeds are removed.” Form: be + past participle. Use the present simple for a general process unless the prompt gives another time frame.

Join stages clearly: “After being sorted, the paper is transported to a mill.” The paper is both sorted and transported, so the subject matches. A relative clause can identify a place: “The paper is sent to a mill, where it is cleaned and pulped.”
WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Active: “A machine washes the bottles and workers sort them by colour.” Passive: “The bottles are washed and then sorted by colour.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  The report focuses on bottles, not who operates each stage. The passive follows “be + past participle” and maintains the same material as subject. Do not make every sentence passive if an active subject such as “water” or “the machine” is useful and shown.
Sequence and alternatives

Useful links: initially; next; after this; once; subsequently; finally. Avoid starting every sentence with “then”. For alternatives: “The photographs can be developed at a pharmacy or by a professional photographer. Alternatively, they can be developed at home.”
For a closed cycle, explain how the final stage leads back to the beginning when this is shown. For a production diagram, do not invent recycling loops, temperatures, machinery or timings.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Two branches after washing: bottles may go directly to filling, or they can be melted and remade. “Once the bottles have been washed, some are refilled directly, whereas others are melted and reshaped.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  “Once” establishes the shared first stage; “whereas” signals two alternative routes. Do not use “finally” for a branch that does not end the whole process. Likewise, describe a loop only if the final arrow actually returns to the beginning.
Plan the details in two groups

Paper recycling: collection, sorting and transport / cleaning, de-inking and paper manufacture. Ketchup: preparing and processing tomatoes / bottling, checking and distribution. Orange juice: shared opening steps and direct packaging / the concentration and reconstitution route.
Now complete E1–E7. Keep the answer key closed until you have attempted each exercise.

WORKED EXAMPLE  •  Diagram: milk production has six stages: feeding cows, milking, cooling, transport, pasteurisation and bottling. Body 1 covers obtaining and storing raw milk; Body 2 covers processing and packaging.

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES  •  Grouping by function makes a six-stage description easier to follow and reduces repeated “then”. The overview can say that raw milk is processed into packaged milk, while the body paragraphs retain the precise order within each group.

Plan information before writing
In Task 1, planning means selecting and grouping what is shown. You do not need to brainstorm opinions or invent examples. Use this worksheet for W1–W11 and for every full writing task.

guide.text: The planning task for W1–W11

For each visual, complete the six worksheet steps. Write a one-sentence introduction and a one- or two-sentence overview. List the two detail-paragraph groups and the main evidence for each. Do not write a full report yet.
Each workshop has a specific focus below. Suggested introductions, overviews, grouping and supporting evidence are all in Part 5. Other accurate groupings are possible.
Progression
W1–W4: charts and comparable tables. W5: a table with different units. W6–W8: maps. W9–W10: mixed visuals. W11: a process. Then use Part 4 to turn the same planning skills into complete reports.
Choose one workshop at a time. Move on when your overview captures the biggest features and each detail group has a clear reason for being together.

small.text: Part 2 Small exercises
E1 · Rewrite trend sentences
Aim: change the grammar while keeping the figures and meaning. Write one sentence for each item using the required opening. Answers are in Part 5, E1.
The share of electricity generated rose from 23% in 1990 to 46% in 2000. Begin: “There was …”
The number of people commuting by car fell from 7,000 in 1990 to 5,000 in 2000. Begin: “A fall …”

E5 · Eight passive sentences
Images are captured by a camera and recorded on film.
The film is removed from the camera.
The film is developed and washed in a development tank in a darkroom.
The negatives are removed from the tank.
The negatives are viewed in an enlarger, where the images can be enlarged and edited.
The images are printed on photographic paper.
The prints are developed, fixed and washed in a chemical bath.

Task 22 · Tomato ketchup production

Task 23 · Energy from coal
Suggested plan: Details 1: coal and oxygen, gas production and purification. Details 2: gas-turbine electricity and heat recovery through the steam turbine.
The diagram shows how coal is used to produce electricity through a system involving gas purification, a gas turbine and a steam turbine.

Overall, coal is converted into a gas that is cleaned before powering a turbine. Heat from the system is also recovered to generate steam, allowing electricity to be produced through a second turbine as well.

Initially, coal and oxygen are supplied to a furnace. Raw syngas is produced, while slag leaves the bottom of the furnace. The gas then passes through a removal stage, where carbon dioxide, mercury and sulphur are separated from it. The resulting purified syngas is directed to a gas turbine, which drives a generator to produce electricity.

Hot exhaust gases are passed to a heat recovery steam generator. This equipment produces steam, which flows to a steam turbine connected to another generator. Electricity is therefore supplied from both generator units. After heat recovery, flue gases leave through the outlet shown above the steam-generating equipment. The diagram thus combines gas-powered generation with the recovery of heat for further electricity production.
Task 24 · Silkworms and silk cloth
Suggested plan: Details 1: the life cycle, including timings and food. Details 2: cocoon selection, boiling, unwinding, twisting, weaving and the two possible dyeing stages.
The diagrams illustrate the life cycle of the silkworm and the stages involved in manufacturing silk cloth.

Overall, the natural cycle runs from eggs to larvae, cocoons and moths, before returning to eggs. Cloth production uses the cocoons as its raw material and involves several processing stages, with dyeing possible at either the thread or cloth stage.

The cycle begins with eggs, which develop into silkworm larvae after about ten days. The larvae feed on mulberry leaves for four to six weeks before producing silk thread. Over the next three to eight days, this thread forms a cocoon. After a further sixteen days, a moth emerges, and eggs are subsequently laid to begin the cycle again.

For silk manufacture, suitable cocoons are first selected and then boiled in water. The silk is unwound from each cocoon, producing a thread approximately 300 to 900 metres long. This thread is twisted and can then be woven into cloth. The diagram also shows that dye can be applied to the twisted thread or to the fabric after weaving.
